PREFACE 


Tlie publication of the Indian Ephemeeis and Nautical Almanac was undertaken in ac car- 
dance with a decision of tbe Government of India, and it marked an important step towards develop- 
ment of astronomical studies in the country. The ephemeris, which was first published in 1957 
for the year 1958, has now stepped into the eighth jmar of publica-tioi^ with the present issue fo 
19G5. 

Astronomical ephembrides containing more or less similar data as in the Indian edition are 
prepared and published by five other countries — ^the United Kingdom, the United States of America > 
France, U.S.S.R., and Spain. There is some uniformity in the contents of all the nationa 
ephemerides although they have undergone considerable changes from time to time. One very^ 
important change, among many others, that" was / introduced in all the ephemerides from the 
issue for 1960, is that the positions of the celestial -bodies -'are now calculated and given according 
to the Ephemeris Time, which is slightly different from the Universal or Greenwich Mean Time. 
This as well as other changes that have been introduced in this publication are discussed below. 

The Greenwich mean time, lately called Universal Time, had so long been the basic measure 
of time in terms of which the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets were calculated and shown 
in the ephemeris. It has been observed for many years past that the rotation of the'Barth, by 
which the Universal Time and in fact all mean solar times are determined, is not uniform ; it has 
got a gradual retardation as well as fluctuations for various reasons, as a result of which the Uni- 
versal Time does not increase uniformly. As a uniformly increasing time-scale is required as the 
independent argument in dynamical astronomy, it has been decided in accordance with a 
resolution of the International Astronomical Union held at Dublin in 1955 that the positioiis of the 
Sun, Moon and planets would be given in all the national ephemerides with effect from the issue 
for 1960, in terms of Ephemeris Time defined by a resolution of the 1952 session of the 
I. A. U. This has been done in all the national ephemerides from the 1960 issue and we have 
also adopted the same. Due to the existence of the fluctuation factor in the rotation of the Earth 
and consequently in the expression for Ephemeris Time, it is not possible to give a definite value 
of E, T. in advance ; it is possible only to estimate an approximate value by extrapolation , 
The excess of E. T. over U. T. has thus been estimated as 35 seconds for 1965 and this value has 
been used in deriving U. T. from E. T. where necessary. The introduction of the ephemeris time 
has also necessitated the adoption of a new reference meridian termed as ephemeris meridian which 
differs from the meridian of Greenwich as the E. T. differs from U. T. The meridian passages of 
the Sun, Moon and planets now given in this publication refer to the time (E. T.) of their passages 
over this ephemeris meridian and not over the meridian of Greenwich. A note dealing with ephe- 
meris time and other related points was given in the Inteoduction to this publication in somewhat 
greater details in the issues for 1960 to 1963, to which a reference may be made by the interested 
readers. 

Pursuant to the above change, the Sidereal Time has been given in a separate table which is 
in terms of U.T. showing the sidereal time for the meridian of Greenwich at O’* U.T. This side- 
real time is identically the same as the sidereal time for the ephemeris meridian at O’* E.T. 
The equation of equinoxes (formerly termed as nutation in R.A.) and the transit of the First 
Point of Aries have also been given in the same table separately. 

Another change irnplicit in the resolution for introduction of the ephemeris time is in respect 
of the mean longitude of the Moon which as given by Brown’s formula requires a correction ; this 
has also been given effect to from the issue for the year 1960 along with the change-over to 
ephemeris time. As regards planets, the positions of the five outer planets, viz., Jupiter, Saturn, 
Uranus", Neptune and Pluto, instead of being derived from the relevant tables are now computed

Five Outer Planets from 1653 to 2060 obtained by numerical integration on the IBM Selective

As regards stars, their mean places and annual proper motions had so long been derived from ■ 
the Third Fundamental Catalogue (FK3). The Fourth Fundamental Catalogue (FKj), the 
preparation of which vas completed at the Astronomisches Bechen Institut in 1961, has been 
adopted for the purpose with effect from the 1964 issue of the publication. The equation of 
time related so long to the equation of ephemeries time, but from the present issue it repre.scnts 
the equation of Universal Time for 0” E.T. 

, The actual calculation and compilation of the figures constituting the different tables of 
an Ephemeris are so laborious and time-consuming that it has been found appropriate to divide 
the labour between the countries that have undertaken the publication of Ephemeris. Thus, each 
of the Xautical Almanac offices mentioned earlier performs a part of the calculations accofding 
to an agreed plan and each country obtains the complete data by exchange with the other countries 
on the basis of an international agreement. According to arrangement, we receive the ephe- 
merides of the Sun and the Moon, major elements of plaiiets, and the Besselian Day Numbers 
from the British Nautical Almanac office, the basic elements of eclipses and data of Moonrise and 
Moonset and of Physical Observations of the Sun and the Moon from the U. S. Naval Observatory , 
and the equatorial co-ordinates of stars from Germany and U. S. S. R. These items of infor- 
mation have either been published in this volume or utilised in making other calculations as required. , 
Our sincere thanks are due to Mr. R. v. d. R. Woolley, the Astronomer Royal and 
to Mr. D. H. Sadler, Superintendent, British Nautical Almanac office who are continuing the 
arrangement. In addition, we have pleasure in acknowledging our indebtedness to Mr. E. W. 
Woolard, Director, American Ephemeris and Nautical Almanac and to the Director of the Nautical 
Almanac office, Leningrad and of the Astronomisches Rechen Institut, Heidelberg, for furnishing 
the advance data from their offices. 

The remaining items of information which are not available in any of the above ephe- 
meridos are calculated at the Nautical Almanac Unit, Calcutta and included in this publication. 
The apparent geocentric longitude and latitude of planets have been calculated and given in 
order to meet the needs of Indian panchang-makors and of many other readers. As regards 
the apparent places of stars, which used to form a part of all the national ephemerides, the 
information is being published, since 1941, as a separate volume under the title Apparent Places 
of Fundamental Stars, which is now issued by the Astronomisches Rechen Institut of Heidelberg, 
Germany. Consequently, the section on this subject has been omitted from some of the national 
ephemerides. In this publication, however, the infoimation relating to apparent places is being 
given in a skeleton form in respect of 68 important stars only, in addition to the mean places 
of 482 stars. The table for mean places include all stars of magnitude up to 3-9 as well as the 
component stars even of magnitude exceeding 3-9 of the different lunar asterisms of the Hindus, 
Chinese and Arabians. In addition to this, the ecliptic co-ordinates (longitude and latitude) of 
the mean places of 46 important star.s with their annual variations and proper motions have also 
been given. The ephemeris transit of the Sun and the "ephemeris of Moon at transit have been 
continued to be included in this publication for facilitating other related ’calculations. The times 
of Moonrise and Moonset for different latitudes, which are- given for the meridian of Greenwich in 
other national ephemerides, are however given in this publication for the central meridian of India 
(82|° E. Longitude). In addition, the times of Sunrise, Sunset and Moonrise, Moonset for some 
Indian cities are given. Some additional items of information are’^also included under eclipses. 
• Tlie co-ordinates of the centre of mass of the solar system, the elements of occultationa of planets 
and bright stars, and precessional elements for reduction of mean places of stars to some back

epochs are specially calculated and included in this publication. The dates of heliacal^ rising 
and setting of the five visible planets and the day of first visibility of the lunar crescent, being the 
requirements of Indian Panchangs, are calculated for the central station of India on the basis 
of some adopted values of the arcs of visibility. 

At present a large number of Almanacs (Paiicangas) are published in India every jmar 
from different parts of the country, giving advance information relating to the longitudes of the 
Sun, Moon, and planets together with other related jihenomena. For their calculations, however, 
the Indian almanac-makers, having been for long left to their own resources and having no astro- 
nomical observatories, had to fall back upon the computational rules developed in India during 
the period 400 to 1200 A. D. These rules with their obvious limitations and errors can hardly be 
expected to give as accurate results as the modern astronomical computations. As a result, the 
planetary positions now given in the Indian almanacs show considerable divergences from the actual 
positions obtained from direct observations or the positions as predicted in the national ephemerides 
This point was illustrated in the Ixtroductiox to the issues for 1958 and 1959. One of the objects 
of preparing this Indian Ephemeris and Naulical Ahnan ac is to in’ovide hccurate data concerning 
the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, computed in accordance with the most up-todate 
astronomical formulae. This publication, therefore, makes available speciall}' to the almanac- 
makers, the astronomical data suited to their requirements, and there should bo no reason any 
longer to continue using astronomically inaqcurale figures for preparing the indigenous almanacs. 

The section on Indian Calendar containing information mostly relating to the Indian calendarial 
system of astronomy has been added to this publication in accordance with the recommendations 
of the Calendar Reform Committee which were accepted by the Government. The calculations 
of the Indian calendar portion are given in Indian Standard Time and the calendar covers an exten- 
ded period up to March 21, 1966, the end of the year 1887 S.E. of the National Calendar of India. 

The significance of the items included in this publication, the methods of the various calcula- 
tions, and explanatory notes on the terms used in the body of the text are given in the Explaxation 
at the end of the book in as much detail as the limitations of space permit. As regards the Indian 
calendar portion, a separate note has been given in Part V to explain the significance of the terms 
used and the basis of different calculations. 

For tendering adviefe regarding development of astronomy and astrophysics in the country, 
the Government of India have set up a ‘Standing Advisory Board for Astronomy’, which is also 
entrusted with the task of advising the India Meteorological Department in its work of compilation 
of the ephemeris. The work of preparing and publishing the Indian Ephemeris and Nautical Almanac 
for 1965 has been under the immediate guidance and supermsion of Shri N. C. Lahiri, M.A., 
Officer-in-charge of the Nautical Almanac Unit, Regional Meteorological Centre, Alipore, Calcutta, 
who also contributed the introductory note on the ephemeris time published in the earlier issues.

CHRONOLOGICAL ERAS 

The year 1887 of the Saka era (Indian Calendar) begins on March 22, 1965. 

The year 2022 of the Vikram Samvat begins on April 2, 1965 (Caitradi), ■ June 30, 1965 
(Asadhadi), or October 25, 1965 (Kartikadi) according to different systems of reckoning. 

The year 1372 of the Bengali San begins on April 14, 1965. 

The year 1141 of the"Kollam era begins on August 16, 1965 (Simhadi) or September 16, 1965 
(Eanyadi) according to different systems of reckoning. 

Barhaspatya varsa (60-year cycle of Jupiter) 52 Kalaynkta begins on January 21, 196.5 
(North Indian usage), and 39 Visvavasu on April 2 or April 13, 1965 (South Indian usage). 

The year 5066 of the Kali era (elapsed) begins on April 15, 1965. 

The year 1385 of the hlohammedan era (the Hejira) begins on May 3, 1965, 

The year 6678 of the Julian period begins on January 14, 1965. 

The year 2741 of the Greek Olympiad, being the 1st year of the 686th Olympiad, begins in 
Jxily, 1965. 

The year 2714 of the Nabouassar era begins on May 2, 1965. 

The year 2277 of the Seleuoidean era begins in the present-day usage of the Syrians on 
September 14 or October 14, 1965 according to different sects. 

The year 19 of the Independence of India begins on August 15, 1965. 

The year 16 of the Republic of India begins on January 26, 1965.

ibove fraction is to be increased by 0-0012. The same may also be obtained by dividing 
lumber of days since 1965.0 by 365.2422.

idar from Chaitra I.

SUNRISE, SUNSET AND MOONRISE,. MOONSET 365 

JIETHOD OF CALCULATION OF SUNEISE AND SUNSET FOR ANY STATION : 

The timings of Sunrise and Sunset have been given at an interval of four days and in local mean 
time of the meridian of Greenwich. The required timing for an intermediate date (not mentioned 
in the table) can easily be obtained by simple interpolation from the figures given at four-day 
intervals. Similarly, the timings for the particular latitude of the station in question (not mentioned 
in the table) can be obtained by simple interpolation between horizontal figures. The table 
on page 363 would, however, facilitate such interpolation for latitude. 

Although the timings are given in the local mean time of the meridian of Greenwich, these can 
be taken as the local mean time for any place on the same latitude without entailing any appreciable 
error. 

The local mean time of Sunrise and Sunset thus obtained for the particular station (if in 
India) can be reduced to the Indian Standard Time bj' applying the time-correction given in the 
reduction table on page 364. 

The beginning of morning twilight and ending of evening twilight can also be similarly calcu- 
lated for any given station. 


For Southern Latitudes 

The timings of Sunrise and Sunset for southern latitudes, which have not been tabulated sepa- 
rately, can be de duced from those for northern latitudes by applying the corrections given in 
pages 340 and 341. 


METHOD OF CALCULATION OF MOONRISE AND MOONSET FOR ANY STATION : 

The timings of Moonrise and Moonset have been given in local mean time calculated for the 
central meridian of India and for latitudes 0° to 50° North, aud also in Indian Standard Time for 
certain stations in India. 

As in the case of Simrise and Sunset, the Moonrise and Moonset times for any particular lati- 
tude of place (within the limits of given latitudes) can be obtained by simple interpolation 
between figures given for the two latitudes — one below and the other above the latitude of the 
station. For this purpose the table on page 363 can also be conveniently made use of. 

The Moonrise and Moonset times given in L.M.T. are exact for the central meridian of India. For 
other meridians the correction given in page 362 should be applied according to the longitude of 
the place and the daily variation of the timing of rising or setting as the case may be. 

By these operations the local mean time of Moonrise and Moonset for the particular latitude 
and longitude of the station concerned is obtained. The Real mean time thus obtained can be 
reduced to the Indian Standard Time by applying the time-correction given in the reduction 
table on page 364. 


For Southern Latitudes 

The timings of Moonriee and Moonset for southern latitudes, which are not tabulated 
separately, can however be deduced from those for the corresponding northern latitudes by the 
formula given below. The error in such a deduction would hardly exceed a minute. 

Timing for a southern latitude

and put a negative sign before it. Then make the number positive by adding the smallest multiple of 1000. The

the required Julian Day Number for the B.C. date.

■INDIAN CALENDAR 


Explanatory Note 

The astronomical data included in this section on Indian Calendar have been calculated in 
accordance with the recommendations of the Calendar Eeform Committee as contained in its 
Report, and the calculations have been made on the basis of the positions of the Sun, Moon and 
planets contained in the main tables of this Ephemeris. Certain additional data which are re- 
quired for the compilation of an Indian Pancanga (Almanac) have also been furnished to meet the 
requirements of the numerous Pajlcaji^a-makers of this country. As the year of the Indian Calendar 
ends on the vernal equinox day, the tables of this section have been extended beyond 1965 to which 
this publication relates, and materials up to March 21, 1966, the next year-ending day of 1887 Saka, 
have been furnished, in order to facilitate preparation of almanacs for one complete Indian year from 
the data given in this publication. The longitudes of the Sun, the Moon and the planets and certain 
other data relating to their positions for the period of 1966 covered by the Indian Calendar portion 
have also been given in separate tables for the same purpose. 

All calculations contained in this section have been made for an adopted Central Station in 
India situated at 82° 30' Longitude East of Greenwich and 23° 11' Latitude North (latitude of 
Ujjain), and accordingly the timings have been expressed in the local mean time of this Central 
Station, which is the Indian Standard Time. The Indian Standard Time (I.S. T.) is 5'“ 30”' ahead 
of the Universal Time or the Greenwich Mean Time. 

V 

The Calendar used in this section is the ‘Indian National Calendar’ as recommended by the 
Calendar Reform Committee and introduced throughout the country by the Government of India 
with effect from the 22nd March, 1957, corresponding to the 1st of Chaitra,' 1879 Saka Era, the 
Indian New Year’s day. The months of this calendar, the number of days assigned to each, and the 
dates of the Gregorian calendar corresponding to the first day of the month are as follows : — '

A description of the different items included in this section is given below : — 

The Sunrise and Sunset times, calculated for the Central Station, relate to the appearance and 
disappearance of the upper limb of the Sun on the horizon. The amount of horizontal refraction 
taken for this purpose is 31' and the semidiameter of the Sun as 16', so that at Sunrise and Sunset 
times the actual centre of the Sun is 47' below the horizon. 


The apparent noon is the local mean time of the Sun’s meridian passage, i.e., the mid-day, 
reduced to the standard meridian of India (82^° E. Longitude). 

The ending moments of tithis and nalcsatras have been given in Indian Standard Time and shown 
against their ordinal numbers. The phenomena being geocentric ones, their timings in I. S. T. 
are applicable for the whole of India without any reduction for. the meridian of other places. 

The tithi is based on the elongation of the Moon from the Sun. A titJd is completed when the 
longitude of the Moon gains exactly 12° or its multiple on that of the Sun, and so there are 30 tithis 
in a lunar month. A ^fference in longitude of 12° indicates the ending of the 1st tithi, 24° that of 
the 2hd tithi, and so on. The nu^ers of tithis have been shown from Sukla 1 to Sukla 15 (full-moon) 
and again from Ki§na 1 to Kr^na 14 and Kr§na 30 (new-moon), using the symbols S and K for Sukla 
(waxing moon) and Er^na (waning moon) respectively. 



INDIAISI CALENBAB- 


391 


As regards naTc§atras, their names have been given at the bottom of the relevant pages^ with 
their numbers. For the purpose of calculation of naksairas, a fixed initial point on the ecliptic has 
been assumed for the measurement of longitudes. This initial point is the same as^ the vernal 
equinoctial point of 285 A.D. For the purpose of assigning a precise position to this fixed initial point 
on the ecliptic, its celestial longitude measured from the true equinox of date has been adopted as 
23° 15' 00" for 21st March, 1956. The longitude of this initial point is known as Ayanamsa. The 
Value of true ayanamsa for the 1st of each month has been shown at the top of the page for the month. 

A nak§atra is completed when the longitude of the Moon measured from the above initial point 
attains a value of 13° 20' or any multiple thereof. When the above difference of longitude is 13°20 
the 1st nak^aira ends, and so on. There are thus 27 naksatras in a sidereal month, and the naksatra 
divisions occupy fixed positions with respect to the stars. In the case of the Sun also the cal- 
culation of naksatras has been done on the same basis. But in that case, the time of Sun's entry into 
a jiaA:faim-division has been shown, whereas in the case of the Moon the time of its exit from 
the division has been given. 

The entry into different Rdsis of the Moon ond the Sun have been shown at the footiiote and the 
calculations have been done on the same basis as in the case of naksatras, A rdsi comprising an 
arc of 30° is measured on the ecliptic from the above-mentioned initial point. 

Tilkis and Naksatras current at sunrise of the Central Station have been shown against the date 
with their ending moments in I, S. T. When the time of these or other phenomena falls after midnight 
and before the next sunrise, 24 hours have been added to the time, without changing the date 
after midnight in order to maintain continuity in time-reckoning from one sunrise to the next in 
conformity with the system followed in Indian religious calendars. 

The solar months for the religious calendar such as Saura Vaiidklia, Saura Jyai§tha, etc., have 
been reckoned from the moments when the apparent longitude of the Sun equals 23° 15', 53°' 15' 
and so on, each differing by 30 degrees. The calculations for this purpose have, thus, been done 
not with a variable ayanamsa as in the case of naksatras, but with a constant ayanamsa of 23° 15'. 

The lunar months necessary for the determination of the dates of religious festivals are 
reckoned from one new- moon to the next (^tikladi or mukJiya nidna). The lunar month is named 
after the saura month in which the initial new-moon falls. 

Phenomena include New-moon, Full-moon, Vyatipata (when the sum of the tropical longitudes 
of the Sun and the Moon equals 180°), Vaidhrti (when the above sum amounts to 360°), eclipses, 
heliacal rising and setting of Jupiter and Yenus, and Jupiter’s transit into rasis. 

All principal festivals of different States have been fixed in accordance with the calculation 
shown in this calendar. In this respect the rules and conventions of the States concerned have 
been followed as far as practicable. 


List op Holidays 

The list of holidays for the Government of India as well as those for all State Governments 
have been prepared in a consolidated form from information as far as available, and dates fixed for 
them have been shown in a' separate table under the head “Principal Festivals for Holidays”. 
The principal festivals of Moslems and Christians have, however, been shown separately. The 
Government of India holidays are given in italics. 

Yogas 

As in the case of naksatras, the ending moments of each of the 27 yogas have also been calculated 
and given in a separate table. The yogas are obtained from the sum of the longitudes of the Moon 
and the Sun, 6ach measured from the fixed initial point mentioned above, and divided into 27 divi- 
sions of 13° 20' each. The names of the 27 yogas have also been given at the bottom of the relevant 
tables. It will be observed that two of the names Vyatipdta and Vaidhrti occur also under Pheno- 
mena, where they have been treated as special yogas and calculated by a somewhat different rule. 
The 21 yogas, which have got very little astronomical significance, have been included in this publi- 
cation in order to meet the needs of a Panmnga of which the yoga is also an essential component. 

Ayanamsa 

The value of true ayanamSa has been given in a separate table at an inteival of three days for 
the period covered by this calendar. , - ■

EXPLANATION 


In the following pages a short explanation of the terms used in this Ephemeris has been given 
and the scope and limitations of the information furnished have been stated in a concise form. The 
values of the different constants and other data upon which the tabiilated quantities are based have 
also been given in some cases in order to facilitate the use of this Ephemerisi But it is not intended 
to furnish here any detailed explanation about the compilation of the tabular matter for which the 
reader is referred to the relevant basic tables and to standard text-books on spherical astronomy. 

TIME 

Formerly, time measured from Greenwich mean noon was known as Greenwich Mean Time. . 
But from 1925 the practice has been changed, and G. M. .T. now denotes the time measured from 
Greenwich mean midnight. The time measured from Greenwich mean noon is now known as Green- 
wich Mean Astronomical Time. Of late, however, the use of the term Greenwich Mean Time has 
been replaced by the term Universal Time in pursuance of a recommendation of the Internationa} 
Astronomical Union (held in 1950). This term (U.T.) has been used in this publication where 
necessar}’’ to denote the Greenwich mean time. 

Apparent Solar Time is the measure of time given by the diurnal motion of the true Sun. It is 
shown by a sundial, but is more correctly measured by the transit of the Sun over the upper meridian 
of a place, at which moment the apparent time is 12“. But due to the existence of various periodic 
terms by which the position of the Sun on the ecliptic is affected, and on account of the ecliptic being 
oblique to the equator, the apparent solar day determined by successive meridian passage? of the Sun 
is not of constant length. With a view to securing a uniform time scale the mean solar time has 
been introduced based on the mean solar day, which is the average of the apparent solar days for a 
long number of years. For the purpose of defining a mean solar day, a fictitious mean sun has 
been conceived moving on the equator with uniform sidereal motion obtaining at 1900-0. Its right 
ascension is very nearly equal to the mean longitude of the Sun affected by mean aberration — differing 
by only a slight, progressivety increasing excess of 0'’-0203 T- due to the secular acceleration of the 
true Sun {T denoting Julian centuries from 1900). Mean Solar Time is determined by the meridian 
transits of this fictitious mean sun, the lower transit marking 0“ and the upper transit 12“ of local 
mean time. The difference between the mean time and the apparent time of any instant is called 
the Equation of Time, so that in the sense in which it is now applied — 

Apparent Time=Mean Time 4-Equation of Time. 

In other words, the equation of time is the hour angle of the true Sun minus the mean astronomical 
time measured from 12“ mean noon. The local mean time of the upper transit of the Sun or the 
mid-day is J3“ — Equation of Time taken for the instant of transit. The equation of time varies 
from — 14^ to4-16| minutes and vanishes four times a year. 

O 

Mean solar time cannot be directly 'determined by observation. It may, however, be 
obtained from the apparent solar time determined by observation of the Sun and correcting the 
same for the equation of time. But on account of the existence of the slight difference between 
the actual mean sun and the fictitious mean sun as defined, the equation of time cannot precisely be 
expressed by its relationship with the mean sun ; and due to non-uniformity of the speed of 
rotation of the Earth the meridian observations of the Sun cannot be utilised. in precise time 
determination. In practice, however, the mean solar time together with the equation of time is 
obtained by calculation from its relation to sidereal time.

EXPLANATION 


Por many years past it has heen noticed that due to irregularities in the rotation of the Earth 
the Universal Time, which is the mean solar time for the meridian of Greenwich, does not increase 
uniformly, and thus makes it difficult for the practical and theoretical work on celestial mechanics 
to be related to the Universal Time. With a view to removing these difficulties, a uniformly 
increasing measure of time termed as Ejtliemeris Time has been introduced in all the. national 
ephemerides including this publication with effect from the issue for the year 1960. Unlike 
Universal Time which is determined by the variable rotation of the Earth, Ephemeris Time is 
determined in principle from the orbital motions of the planets, specially the orbital motion of the 
Earth. In practice, however, it is obtained from observations of the Moon as the Moon’s motion 
in its orbit is by far the fastest available. Ephemeris Time is thus the measure of time in terms 
of which the positions of celestial bodies determined from dynamical astronomy agree with 
observation. 

The fundamental epoch from which Ephemeris Time is reckoned is the instant near the 
beginning of the year 1900 when the geometric mean longitude of the Sun referred to the mean 
equinox of date was 279° 41' 48. "04, this instant being designated as 1900, January 0, 12^ E.T. 
This epoch is about 4 secs, later than 12'* U. T. The ephemeris seeond is defined as 
1/31556925.9747 of the tropical year for 1900, January 0, 12” E.T. The ephemeris day is 86400 
ephemeris seconds. These give the increase of the mean longitude of the Sun per century of 36525 
ephemeris days at 1900, Jan. 0, 12” E.T. as 129602768. "13 which is assumed to be an invariable. 
In fact Ephemeris Time is the measure of time in which Newcomb’s Tables of the Sun agree with 
observation. Along with the ephemeris time a new fictitious prime meridian termed as Ephemeris 
Meridian has also been introduced for measuring longitudes of stations on the Earth required in 
some calculations. The longitude measured from this ephemeris meridian has been termed , as 
Ephemeris Longitude of the station. The new time measure and other related changes introduced 
from the issue for 1960 have been discussed in greater details in the Inteoduction to this 
publication for the years 1960 to 1963 to which a reference may be made. 

The relation between Ephemeris Time and Universal Time is

obtained by calculation, it is only to be determined by analysis of observations over a more or less 
extended period.

Sidereal Time 

Sidereal Time is the measure of time defined by the diurnal motion of the vernal equinox. Un- 
like the mean and the apparent solar times, which are both measured ftom the instant of the 
lower meridian transit, sidereal time is still measured from the upper transit of the First Point of 
Aries (vernal equinoctial point), at which moment the sidereal time is O'*. It is determined from 
observations of meridian transits of known stars. Because of the accuracy with which it can be 
determined by observation, sidereal time is the primary astronomical measure of time. As the 
equinox oscillates about its mean position due to the effect of nutation, the sidereal time measured 
from the meridian transit of the equinox is also of two kinds : the apparent sidereal time and the 
mean or uniform sidereal time, the former being obtained from the transit of the true equinox and 
the latter from that of the mean equinox. The relation between the two is — 

Apparent Sidereal Time= Mean or Uniform Sidereal Time+Equation of Equinoxes. 

The value of the equation of equinoxes , which was previously termed as nutation in R.A., varies 
within +1-2 seconds of time in a period of 18.6 years.

EQUINOXES 

The vernal equinox or the First Point of Aries, which is the fundamental origin from which right 
ascensions and celestial longitudes are measured, is not fixed among the stars, but has a nearly uniform 
retrograde motion of about 50"'3 per year due to precession of the equinoxes, and an oscillatory 
motion due to nutation. This gives rise to the mean equinox of date and the true or apparent 
equinox. Similarly, the inclination of the ecliptic to the equator, known as the obliquity of the 
ecliptic, is also variable. The inclination suffers a slow uniform diminution of about half a second 
per year as well as an oscillation due to nutation in obliquity. 

The position of the mean equinox at the beginning of the Besselian fictitious year (tlie moment 
when the right ascension of the mean sun, affected by aberration and measured from the mean equinox, 
is'2S0° or IS** 40“) is known as the mean equinox of the beginning of the year, or more briefly, for 
the year 1965, as the equinox of 19G5'0. For the purpose of observation, the positions of heavenly 
bodies must clearly be referred to the apparent or true equinox of date, and accordingly aU quantities 
in this Ephemeris are referred to this equinox unless otherwise stated. For theoretical work, how- 
ever, the mean equinox of date or that for the beginning of the .year is convenient. An equinox 
that can be used unchanged for a long period has, however, been foxmd more useful in some kind of 
work ; for this purpose the equinox of 1950-0 has been adopted which will serve for some years more. 

The expressions for nutation in longitude and in obliquity consist of a number of periodic 
terms ; those depending'upon the longitude of the Moon’s Node and the, elements of. the Sun are 
known as terms of long period, since defined as having a period of 100 days or more, and those

Aberration 

For the Sun and planets aberration is the displacement of the body during the time taken by 
light to travel from the body to the Earth. It is known as flanetary aberration. The apparent 
position of a heavenly body is that which the body occupied when the light left it and the true 
position is the actual position that it occupies at the time of observation. The apparent 
positionis behind the true position of the body by the amount of aberration. The constant of 
aberration is 20"' 47 being equivalent to a light time of 498^-38 for unit distance (mean distance of the 
Sun). The aberration correction, to be applied to either coordinate relating to the true position of 
a member of the solar system to obtain its apparent position, is 

— 0-0057683 X distance from the Earth xjxmotion in d days. 

For most planets d is taken to be 2, giving the correction as 

— 0-0028841 X distance from the Earth X motion in 2 days. 

In the case of the Sun, however, when extreme accuracy is not required, the aberration may 
be obtained from 20"-47-{-0''-34 cos g or more correctly from 20"‘47 divided by the radius’ vector. 

In the case of a star, the aberration of light known as stellar aberration is due to the velocity 
of the Earth in its orbit relative to the velocity of light coming from the star. This relative motion 
of the observer causes a deflection of the apparent direction of the star towards the apex of the 
Earth’s orbit or the direction in which the Earth is moving which is 90° behind the Sun. In this 
case the maximum deflection is the same as the constant of aberration of 20".47 for the mean 
velocity of the Earth. The stellar aberration resolves into two parts: one, contributed by the 
circular motion of the Earth moving with a constant mean velocity round the Sun, and the other, a 
constant displacement perpendicular to the major axis of the orbit, which being a nearly constant 
quantity is included in the mean position of the star.

Apparent Place 

Tbe apparent place of a heavenly body is its position corrected for precession and nutation, so 
that it is referred to tbe true equinox and equator (or ecliptic) of date, and it is also corrected for 
aberration. It is tbus tbe position in wbicb tbe body would be seen by an observer situated at 
tbe centre of tbe Eartb. But for an observer on tbe surface of tbe Eartb tbe results of observation 
will bave to be corrected for atmospheric refraction, parallax, and diurnal aberration (when necessary) 
in order to obtain tbe geocentric apparent place as mentioned above. In case of tbe Sun and the 
planets tbe position unaffected by aberration is the true position for tbe moment, wbicb tbe body 
actually occupies at that time. In case of stars, tbe mean place for a particular equinox, e.g., for 
1950*0 is tbe position of tbe star on tbe date in question but referred to tbe mean equinox specified. 
Tbe apparent place of a star for any date is obtained by tbe application of proper motion, pro- 
cession, nutation, stellar aberration and annual parallax (where appreciable) to its mean position.

equinox of 1950-0 and then subtracting the stellar aberration pertinent to the position occupied, bv 
the planet, calculated by the conventional formula which neglects the portion depending on the 
longitude of the Earth’s perihelion. The astrometric place is thus affected by the amount of the 
terms in the aberration dependent on the longitude of the Earth’s perihelion as are the catalogue 
mean places of stars in the neighbourhood. The astrometric ephemeris is therefore rigorously 
comparable with photographic observations that are referred to catalogue mean places (1950-0) 
of neighbouring stars, it being only necessary to correct the observations for geocentric parallax 
in case of the planet and proper motion in case of the stars. 

The tabular true distance from the Earth is the actual geocentric distance at ths tabular 
time and not at the instant when the light left the planet.

The Osculating Elements of the orbits of the five outer planets are given at intervals of 80 
days. The osculating elements are the elements of the instantaneous elliptic orbit of the planet 
about the Sun determined by its actual position and velocity components for the instant, and 
as such the elements are affected by the attractions of other planets. The true place of a 
planet deduced from these elements is thus inclusive of the planetary perturbations, vrhich need 
not, therefore, be considered separately in such a deduction. The mean elements of the planetary 
orbits given on page ix may be considered as the mean of the corresponding osculating 
elements taken over a very long period and are thus independent of the effects of other planets 
except for secular changes. ' '

The Besselian Day Numbers for each day of the year, the Mean Places of certain stars (482

day of the year have been given in this section. ' The table for Mean Places of Stars include all stars

Hindus, Chinese and Arabians even when the magnitudes of such stars exceed 3*9. The celestial

E'phemerides for Physical Ohsermtions of the Swi and the Moon 

Tbe Sun rotates about its axis westward in a sidereal period of 25.38 mean solar days. The 
in synodic period of j;otation is however 27.2753 days. Tbe standard solar meridian from 
icb heliograpbio longitudes on tbe surface of the Sun are measured (positive towards tbe west) 
^bat which passed through tbe ascending node of tbe solar equator on tbe ecliptic on 1854 
luary 1, Greenwich mean noon. Tbe beginning of each synodic rotation given in tbe table on 
;e 320 is tbe instant at which tbe standard solar meridian passes through tbe central point of 
apparent disc of tbe Sun, f .e., when tbe beliograpbic longitude of this central point is zero. 

In case of tbe Moon, selenograpbic longitudes are measured for a point on tbe surface of tbe • 
on from the lunar meridian tbat passes through tbe mean central point of tbe visible disc, 
litive towards tbe west. .Selenograpbic latitudes are reckoned positive towards tbe north 
b. Tbe mean central point of tbe disc is defined as tbe point on tbe lunar surface intersected 
tbe radius of tbe Moon directed towards tbe Earth, when tbe Moon is simultaneously at either 
the mean nodes and mean apsidal points of tbe lunar orbiti 
Tbe tabular selenograpbic longitude and latitude of tbe Earth are tbe selenograpbic co- 
liuates of tbe apparent central poiut of tbe disc of tbe j\Ioon from which point tbe Earth 
in selenograpbic zenith.. These co-ordinates are tbe total librations (sums of optical and 
ysical librations) in longitude and latitude respectively. MTien tbe libratiou in longitude, I'.e., tbe 
snograpbic longitude of tbe Earth, is positive, tbe mean central point of tbe disc is displaced 
itward exposing to view a region on tbe west limb. lYben tbe libration in latitude, i.e., tbe 
enograpbic latitude of tbe Earth, is positive, a region on tbe north limb is exposed to view. 

Tbe selenograpbic co-ordinates of tbe point on tbe lunar surface where tbe Sun is in zenith 
s tbe selenograpbic co-ordinates of tbe Sun. The selenograpbic co-Iongitiide of tbe Sun tabulated' 
tbe epbemeris is obtained by subtracting tbe seienograpbic longitude of tbe Sun from 90° or 450° ; 
is approximately 270°, 0°, 90°, and 180° at new-moori, first quarter, full-moon, and last quarter 
ipectively. 

Tbe position angle of tbe axis is tbe angle tbat tbe lunar meridian through tbe apparent ' 
atral point of tbe disc towards tbe north lunar pole forms with tbe declination circle through tbe 
atial point, reckoned eastward from tbe north point of the disc. 

Tbe position angle of tbe Bright Limb is tbe position angle of tbe midpoint of tbe illuminated 
ab, reckoned eastward from the jwith point of the disc. Tbe position angles of tbe two cusps may 
obtained by adding ^90° to tbat of tbe bright limb. 

Sunrise, Sunset, Twilight, Moonrise and Moonset

nple interpolation for tbe desired latitude within tbe scope of tbe tables, are in local mean time 
tbe place. Strictly speaking, tbe timings of Sunrise, Sunset and Twibgbt are for places on the

‘At the given times of Sunrise and Sunset the upper limb of the Sun is on the horizon ; the true 
zenith distance of the Sun’s centre is then taken as 90° 50', allowing 16' for semi-diameter and 34' 
for horizontal refraction. 

The timings of the beginning of morning twilight and en<hng of eyening twilight relate to the 
instants when the centre of the Sun is 18° below the horizon. This is now known as astronomical 
twilight. The period of twilight has been divided into three parts— Civil when the Sun is 6° below 
the horizon, Nautical when 12° and Astronomical when 18°— and their durations have been given. 

The .Sunrise and Sunset times for certain stations in India (Calcutta, Varanasi, Madras, Delhi 
and Bombay) have been separately computed and given in Indian Standard Time. In these cal- 
culations the amount of horizontal refraction has been taken as 31', the value derived from considera- 
tion of the atmospheric conditions in India, and consequently the zenith. distance of the Sun’s centre 
is 90° 47' at the times given. In the section on Indian Calendar, the Sunrise and Sunset times given 
for latitude 23° 11' North and the Central Meridian of India also relate to the times when the upper 
limb of the Sun is on the horizon as in the general tables.

Paet V — ^Indian Calendar 

'The soope and tHe significance of the information furnished in the section on Indian Calendaf 
have been stated in an Explanatory Note on pages 390 and 391 at the beginning of the section. All 
calculations of this section have been done for a Central Station in India (82° 30' E. Long, and 
23* 11' N, Lat.) and the results are given in Indian Standard Time. 

For.the calculation of rd^is and 'nah^atras of this section, a fixed initial point on the ecliptic 
has been taken as the origin from 'which the longitudes are measured for this purpose. The tropical 
longitude of this initial point for March 21, 1956 is adopted as 23° 15' 0".0. The longitude of this 
initial point is known as ayanamsa in Indian astronomy and is to be subtracted from the tropical 
(or sdyana) longitudes of celestial objects to obtain the corresponding nirayana longitudes of 
Indian astronomy. The value of mean ayanamsa for any date may be obtained from the following 
formula : 

A=22° 27' 37"-69+5025”'64 T+1"-111T^

Heliacal Rising and Selling of Planets 

The planets Mercury to Saturn (as well as the Moon) remain invisible to the naked eye for 
some days at the time of conjuction with the Sun. This phenomenon of planet’s in'visibility due 
to its proximity to the Sun is known as combust or heliacal setting of the planet, and it plays an 
important part in Indian Calendar. The dates of heliacal setting and rising of the planets marking 
the period of invisibility have been calculated assuming that the phenomenon occurs when, at the 
given station, the Sun attains a zenith distance of 90°+/i at the time when the zenith distance of 
the planet is 90°. The values of li for different planets adopted for the purpose are as follows : 

Mercury 10° (Direct) and 11° (Retrograde) 

Venus 6°, Mars 14°, Jupiter 8°.5, and Saturn 12° 

The figures for Mercury have been revised on the basis of observation and the new values have 
been adopted with effect from May, 1964. 

The day of first visibility of the lunar crescent after a uew-moon day has also been determined 
in a somewhat similar way on the basis of the following values of the limiting altitude of the Moon 
above the horizon corresponding to its azimuth difference from the Sun, when the zenith distance 
of the Sun is 90°. 

Azimuth difference . 0° 5° 10° 15° 20° 

/ • Altitude . . . 10°-4 10°-0 9°-3 8°-0 6°-2 

When the altitude of the Moon at Sunset exceeds the above limit, the Moon is expected to be 
visible in that evening. The beginnings of months of the Islamic calendar have been determined 
on the basis of the above calculations; 

■ The computations of heliacal risings and settings of planets and determination of the dates 
of first visibility of the Moon have been done for the Central Station of India.
